statement: Let $B = A^{\mathrm{co}H}$ for a right $H$-[comodule algebra](c:comodule-algebra) $A$ over a [Hopf algebra](c:hopf-algebra) $H$. If $B \subseteq A$ is [Hopf-Galois](c:hopf-galois-extension) and $A$ is [faithfully flat](c:faithfully-flat) over $B$, then $N \mapsto N \otimes_B A$ is an equivalence from right $B$-modules to relative Hopf modules $\mathcal{M}_A^H$, with inverse $M \mapsto M^{\mathrm{co}H}$.

hypotheses.text: $A$ is a right $H$-[comodule algebra](c:comodule-algebra) over a [Hopf algebra](c:hopf-algebra) $H$ over a commutative ring $k$, and $B = A^{\mathrm{co}H}$.
The extension $B \subseteq A$ is [Hopf-Galois](c:hopf-galois-extension): the canonical map $A \otimes_B A \to A \otimes H$, $a \otimes a' \mapsto a\,a'_{(0)} \otimes a'_{(1)}$, is bijective.
$A$ is [faithfully flat](c:faithfully-flat) as a left $B$-module.

conclusion: The functor $N \mapsto N \otimes_B A$ is an [equivalence of categories](c:equivalence-of-categories) from right $B$-modules onto $\mathcal{M}_A^H$, with quasi-inverse $M \mapsto M^{\mathrm{co}H}$.

proofs.name: Faithfully flat descent
proofs.slogan: Relative Hopf modules are descent data for $B \subseteq A$, and faithfully flat descent turns these into $B$-modules.
proofs.scope: The right-right version of the theorem, over any commutative ring $k$. Schneider's other equivalent conditions (projectivity of $A$ over $B$, injectivity of $A$ as a comodule) are not proved here.

roles.why: The coaction of $H$ on $A$ and the invariants $B$ define both the Galois map and the Hopf modules.
The bijective Galois map identifies the coring $A \otimes H$ with the Sweedler [coring](c:coring) $A \otimes_B A$, so Hopf modules become descent data.
Faithful flatness is exactly the condition under which descent data are equivalent to $B$-modules.

steps.slogan: Form the Sweedler [coring](c:coring) $A \otimes_B A$ of the extension.
steps.detail: The $A$-bimodule $C = A \otimes_B A$ is an $A$-[coring](c:coring) with coproduct $a \otimes a' \mapsto a \otimes 1 \otimes a'$ and the multiplication as counit. Its comodules are the descent data for $B \subseteq A$, and $N \otimes_B A$ is such a comodule for every right $B$-module $N$.

steps.slogan: Transport the $H$-coaction through the Galois map.
steps.detail: The canonical map $A \otimes_B A \to A \otimes H$ is an isomorphism of $A$-corings, where $A \otimes H$ has the coproduct that comes from that of $H$. A relative Hopf module $M$ has a coaction $M \to M \otimes H \cong M \otimes_A (A \otimes H)$, which the isomorphism turns into a map $M \to M \otimes_B A$.

steps.slogan: Show that relative Hopf modules are exactly the descent data.
steps.detail: The coaction is coassociative and counital exactly when its transport to $M \otimes_B A$ is, because the canonical map respects coproducts and counits. So $\mathcal{M}_A^H$ is isomorphic to the category of descent data, and the coinvariants $M^{\mathrm{co}H}$ correspond to the equalizer of the descent datum.

steps.slogan: Apply [faithfully flat descent](c:faithfully-flat-descent) to the descent data.
steps.detail: Because $A$ is [faithfully flat](c:faithfully-flat) as a left $B$-module, the functor $N \mapsto N \otimes_B A$ is comonadic, by the dual of Beck's monadicity theorem. So it is an equivalence from right $B$-modules onto descent data, and its inverse takes the equalizer of the descent datum.

steps.slogan: Read the inverse as the functor of coinvariants.
steps.detail: Under the isomorphism of step 3, the equalizer of the descent datum of $M$ is $M^{\mathrm{co}H} = \{m : \rho(m) = m \otimes 1\}$. So $M^{\mathrm{co}H} \otimes_B A \to M$ and $N \to (N \otimes_B A)^{\mathrm{co}H}$ are isomorphisms, and the equivalence has the stated inverse.

concepts.c:comodule-algebra: The algebra $A$ with its coaction carries the Hopf modules and the invariants $B$.
concepts.c:hopf-algebra: The Hopf algebra $H$ supplies the coaction and the coproduct that the Galois map transports.
concepts.c:hopf-galois-extension: The Galois bijection turns Hopf modules into descent data for $B \subseteq A$.
concepts.c:faithfully-flat: Faithful flatness makes descent data equivalent to modules over $B$.
concepts.c:equivalence-of-categories: The theorem states an equivalence between $B$-modules and relative Hopf modules.
concepts.c:coring: The Sweedler coring encodes descent data as comodules over $A \otimes_B A$.
concepts.c:faithfully-flat-descent: Faithfully flat descent gives the equivalence between descent data and $B$-modules.

source.note: As on nLab: relative Hopf modules are descent data for the Hopf-Galois extension, so Schneider's theorem (Israel J. Math. 72, 1990) reduces to faithfully flat descent, in Schauenburg's form.

statement: For squarefree $d > 0$, the [imaginary quadratic field](c:imaginary-quadratic-field) $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-d})$ has trivial [ideal class group](c:ideal-class-group) if and only if $d \in \{1, 2, 3, 7, 11, 19, 43, 67, 163\}$. Equivalently, its ring of integers is a principal ideal domain exactly for these nine fields.

hypotheses.text: The field is $K = \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-d})$ for a squarefree integer $d > 0$, an [imaginary quadratic field](c:imaginary-quadratic-field).

conclusion: $K$ has class number $1$ exactly when $d$ is one of $1, 2, 3, 7, 11, 19, 43, 67, 163$.

proofs.name: Heegner-Stark modular proof
proofs.slogan: Genus theory and complex multiplication turn class number one into integrality of $j$, and Heegner's modular argument excludes all discriminants below $-163$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, as an outline: steps 3 and 4 rest on the cited work. The related problems of class number two and higher (Baker, Stark, Goldfeld, Gross-Zagier) are not covered.

roles.why: The discriminant $D$ of $K$ is the object that genus theory, complex multiplication and the reduced-form count all use.

steps.slogan: Use genus theory to restrict the discriminant of a field of class number one.
steps.detail: Genus theory shows that $2^{t-1}$ divides the class number when the discriminant $D$ has $t$ prime divisors. So class number one forces $D \in \{-4, -8\}$ or $D = -p$ with $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$ prime.

steps.slogan: Turn class number one into an integrality statement about the $j$-invariant.
steps.detail: The value $j(\tau_D)$ of the [modular function](c:modular-function) $j$ at $\tau_D = (D + \sqrt{D})/2$ is an algebraic integer of degree $h(D)$ over $\mathbb{Q}$. So $h(D) = 1$ makes $j(\tau_D)$ a rational integer.

steps.slogan: Rewrite the integrality of $j$ through Weber's modular functions.
steps.detail: Heegner (1952) and Stark (1967) express $j(\tau_D)$ by Weber's functions and use their modular equation. For class number one this gives an integer solution of an explicit Diophantine equation attached to $D$.

steps.slogan: Show that this equation has no solution when $D < -163$.
steps.detail: The cited work compares the $q$-expansion estimate $j(\tau_D) \approx -e^{\pi\sqrt{|D|}}$ with the shape that the equation forces on the integer solution. Stark's analysis closes the gap in Heegner's argument and excludes every $D < -163$.

steps.slogan: Verify the nine fields directly and combine this with the exclusion of all others.
steps.detail: For $D = -3, -4, -7, -8, -11, -19, -43, -67, -163$, every reduced form $ax^2 + bxy + cy^2$ with $|b| \le a \le c$ and $b^2 - 4ac = D$ is the principal form, so $h(D) = 1$. Steps 1 to 4 show that no other field has class number one.

concepts.c:imaginary-quadratic-field: The theorem classifies these fields by their class number.
concepts.c:ideal-class-group: Class number one means that this group is trivial.
concepts.c:modular-function: The $j$-function is the modular function whose values at $\tau_D$ carry the class number.

source.ref: H. M. Stark, A complete determination of the complex quadratic fields of class-number one, Michigan Mathematical Journal 14 (1967), 1-27
source.note: Outline of the modular proof of Heegner (1952), completed by Stark (1967, 1969); Baker (1966) gave an independent proof with linear forms in logarithms.

statement: Let $X$, $Y$, $Z$ be [complete varieties](c:complete-variety) over an algebraically closed field, and $L$ a [line bundle](c:line-bundle) on $X \times Y \times Z$. If the restrictions of $L$ to $\{x_0\} \times Y \times Z$, $X \times \{y_0\} \times Z$ and $X \times Y \times \{z_0\}$ are trivial, then $L$ is trivial.

hypotheses.text: The varieties $X$, $Y$, $Z$ are irreducible [complete varieties](c:complete-variety) over an algebraically closed field $k$.
For points $x_0, y_0, z_0$, the restrictions of $L$ to the three slices through them are trivial.

conclusion: The [line bundle](c:line-bundle) $L$ on $X \times Y \times Z$ is trivial.

proofs.name: Seesaw, curve and rigidity
proofs.slogan: Reduce to a curve in the first factor, map the other two factors to its Jacobian, and use rigidity to show that this map is zero.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for three complete varieties. Mumford's sharper form, in which $Z$ is any connected variety, is not proved here.

roles.why: Completeness of $Y \times Z$ gives the seesaw, completeness of $X$ gives curves through two points, and completeness of $Y$ gives rigidity.
The three trivial slices make the map to the Jacobian well defined, zero on two axes, and force the base bundle to be trivial.

steps.slogan: Reduce the claim to triviality on each slice $\{x\} \times Y \times Z$.
steps.detail: The seesaw theorem for the complete variety $Y \times Z$ over the base $X$ says: if $L$ is trivial on $\{x\} \times Y \times Z$ for every $x$, then $L \cong p_1^* M$ with $M = L|_{X \times \{(y_0, z_0)\}}$. This $M$ is trivial because it is a restriction of the trivial slice $X \times \{y_0\} \times Z$, so $L$ is trivial.

steps.slogan: Replace $X$ by a smooth complete curve through $x_0$ and a given point $x_1$.
steps.detail: Any two points of a complete variety lie on an irreducible curve $C \subseteq X$ (Bertini's theorem for projective varieties, Chow's lemma in general). Pull $L$ back to the normalization $\tilde C$ of $C$; the three slice conditions persist. It now suffices to show that $L$ is trivial on $\tilde C \times Y \times Z$.

steps.slogan: Map $Y \times Z$ to the Jacobian of the curve using $L$.
steps.detail: Put $T = Y \times Z$ and let $J = \mathrm{Pic}^0(\tilde C)$ be the [Jacobian](c:jacobian-variety) of $\tilde C$, an [abelian variety](c:abelian-variety). The bundle $L$ is trivial on $\{x_0\} \times T$ and has degree $0$ on $\tilde C \times \{t\}$ for every $t$, since $T$ is connected and the degree is $0$ at $(y_0, z_0)$. So $L$ defines a morphism $\varphi\colon T \to J$.

steps.slogan: Apply the rigidity lemma to show that $\varphi$ is zero.
steps.detail: On $Y \times \{z_0\}$ the bundle is trivial, so $\varphi(y, z_0) = 0$ for all $y$. Since $Y$ is complete, the rigidity lemma gives $\varphi(y, z) = \varphi(y_0, z)$ for all $y, z$. The slice $\tilde C \times \{y_0\} \times Z$ is trivial, so $\varphi(y_0, z) = 0$. Hence $\varphi = 0$.

steps.slogan: Conclude with the seesaw theorem over $T$ and the reduction of step 1.
steps.detail: Since $\varphi = 0$, $L$ is trivial on $\tilde C \times \{t\}$ for every $t \in T$. The seesaw theorem with complete fibre $\tilde C$ gives $L|_{\tilde C \times T} \cong p_T^* N$ with $N = L|_{\{x_0\} \times T}$ trivial. So $L$ is trivial on $\{x_1\} \times Y \times Z$ for every $x_1$, and step 1 finishes the proof.

concepts.c:complete-variety: Completeness supplies the seesaw theorem, curves through two points and the rigidity lemma.
concepts.c:line-bundle: The theorem asks for triviality of this line bundle, which the proof tests slice by slice.
concepts.c:jacobian-variety: The Jacobian of the curve receives the map that records the family of slices.
concepts.c:abelian-variety: The Jacobian is an abelian variety, so the rigidity lemma applies to maps into it.

source.note: The seesaw and rigidity argument of the standard proof (Mumford, Abelian Varieties, sections 5 and 10), in the form that reduces to a curve and uses its Jacobian.

statement: Let $A_i \subseteq R_i$ be open, and $\Pi^r$ the [restricted product](c:restricted-product). For a space $Y$, a map $f\colon Y \times \Pi^r \to X$ is continuous iff it is continuous on $Y \times \Pi_S$ for every cofinite $S$. Here $\Pi_S = \prod_{i \notin S} R_i \times \prod_{i \in S} A_i$ has the [product topology](c:product-topology).

hypotheses.text: Each $A_i$ is an open subset of $R_i$.
$Y$ and $X$ are arbitrary [topological spaces](c:topological-space), not necessarily locally compact.

conclusion: The map $f$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function) exactly when every restriction $f|_{Y \times \Pi_S}$, for $S$ cofinite, is continuous.

proofs.name: Open pieces and neighborhood filters
proofs.slogan: Each piece $\Pi_S$ is open in the restricted product, so neighborhoods of a point of $Y \times \Pi^r$ come from a piece.
proofs.scope: The whole equivalence, with no assumption on $Y$. The indexed family may be empty or finite, and then $\Pi^r$ is the full product.

roles.why: Openness of the $A_i$ makes every $\Pi_S$ an open subspace of $\Pi^r$.
Neighborhoods in a product of arbitrary spaces are products, so no local compactness of $Y$ is needed.

steps.slogan: Restrict a continuous map along the continuous inclusions.
steps.detail: For each cofinite $S$, the inclusion $\Pi_S \to \Pi^r$ is continuous, because the topology of $\Pi^r$ is built from these pieces. So $\mathrm{id} \times \mathrm{incl}$ is continuous, and $f \circ (\mathrm{id} \times \mathrm{incl})$ is continuous. This proves the forward direction.

steps.slogan: Fix a point and find a cofinite set where its coordinates are restricted.
steps.detail: Take $(y, x) \in Y \times \Pi^r$. By definition of $\Pi^r$, $x_i \in A_i$ for all but finitely many $i$. The set $S = \{i : x_i \in A_i\}$ is cofinite, and $x = \mathrm{incl}(x')$ for a point $x' \in \Pi_S$.

steps.slogan: Show that the inclusion of $\Pi_S$ is an open embedding.
steps.detail: Because each $A_i$ is open, $\Pi_S$ is an open subset of $\Pi^r$ and carries the subspace topology. Hence the [neighborhood](c:neighborhood) filter of $x = \mathrm{incl}(x')$ is the image of the neighborhood filter of $x'$ under $\mathrm{incl}$.

steps.slogan: Write the neighborhood filter of the pair as a product of filters.
steps.detail: In any product, the neighborhoods of $(y, x)$ are generated by the products $U \times V$. So $\mathcal{N}(y, x) = \mathcal{N}(y) \times \mathrm{incl}_*\,\mathcal{N}(x') = (\mathrm{id} \times \mathrm{incl})_*\,\mathcal{N}(y, x')$. This uses no assumption on $Y$.

steps.slogan: Transfer continuity of the restriction to continuity of $f$ at the point.
steps.detail: Continuity of $f \circ (\mathrm{id} \times \mathrm{incl})$ at $(y, x')$ says that it sends $\mathcal{N}(y, x')$ into $\mathcal{N}(f(y, x))$. By step 4 this says that $f$ sends $\mathcal{N}(y, x)$ into $\mathcal{N}(f(y, x))$. So $f$ is continuous at the arbitrary point $(y, x)$.

steps.slogan: Join the two directions into the stated equivalence.
steps.detail: The forward direction is step 1 and the reverse direction is step 5. Hence $f$ is continuous if and only if every restriction $f|_{Y \times \Pi_S}$ is continuous.

concepts.c:restricted-product: The map is defined on a product with this space, which is the union of the pieces $\Pi_S$.
concepts.c:product-topology: Each piece $\Pi_S$ and the product $Y \times \Pi^r$ carry product topologies.
concepts.c:topological-space: The parameter space $Y$ and the target $X$ are arbitrary spaces.
concepts.c:continuous-function: The theorem tests continuity of $f$ through its restrictions.
concepts.c:neighborhood: Continuity at a point is tested on neighborhood filters, which pass through the open embedding.

source.note: mathlib uses the open embedding of each piece (isOpenEmbedding_inclusion_principal, nhds_eq_map_inclusion) and the product of neighborhood filters (nhds_prod_eq, prod_map_map_eq).

statement: Let $f\colon G \to H \times I$ be a [monoid homomorphism](c:monoid-hom). If the first coordinate of $f$ is surjective onto $H$, and equal first coordinates force equal second coordinates, then the image of $f$ is the [graph of a function](c:graph-of-a-function) $f'\colon H \to I$, and $f'$ is a monoid homomorphism.

hypotheses.text: The map $f\colon G \to H \times I$ is a [monoid homomorphism](c:monoid-hom).
The first coordinate $\mathrm{pr}_1 \circ f\colon G \to H$ is surjective.

conclusion: There is a monoid homomorphism $f'\colon H \to I$ whose graph, a [submonoid](c:submonoid) of $H \times I$, equals the image of $f$.

formal.difference: The declaration is the additive form of the lemma, for additive monoids. The multiplicative form MonoidHom.exists_mrange_eq_mgraph states the result as written here.

proofs.name: Read off the second coordinate
proofs.slogan: Define $f'$ by taking the second coordinate over any preimage of $h$, then check the graph and the homomorphism laws.
proofs.scope: The whole statement for monoids. The empty case does not arise, since monoids have an identity element.

roles.why: Multiplicativity of $f$ gives $f(1) = (1, 1)$ and $f(g_1 g_2) = f(g_1) f(g_2)$, which make $f'$ a homomorphism.
Surjectivity gives a preimage for every $h \in H$, so $f'$ is defined everywhere and the graph is the whole image.
The vertical line condition makes the value of $f'$ independent of the chosen preimage.

steps.slogan: Define $f'$ by reading the second coordinate along any preimage.
steps.detail: For $h \in H$, surjectivity gives $g \in G$ with $f(g)_1 = h$. Set $f'(h) = f(g)_2$. The vertical line condition makes this value independent of the choice of $g$, so $f'$ is a well-defined function.

steps.slogan: Show that the image of $f$ is the [graph of the function](c:graph-of-a-function) $f'$.
steps.detail: Each $f(g)$ equals $(f(g)_1, f'(f(g)_1))$ by the definition of $f'$, so the image lies in the graph. Conversely, for $h \in H$ pick $g$ with $f(g)_1 = h$; then $(h, f'(h)) = f(g)$ lies in the image.

steps.slogan: Show that $f'$ sends the identity to the identity.
steps.detail: The identity of $G$ has $f(1) = (1, 1)$, because $f$ is a monoid homomorphism. Its first coordinate is $1$, so $f'(1) = f(1)_2 = 1$.

steps.slogan: Show that $f'$ respects products.
steps.detail: For $h_1, h_2 \in H$ choose $g_1, g_2$ with $f(g_k)_1 = h_k$. Then $f(g_1 g_2) = f(g_1) f(g_2)$ has first coordinate $h_1 h_2$ and second coordinate $f'(h_1) f'(h_2)$. By the definition of $f'$, $f'(h_1 h_2) = f'(h_1) f'(h_2)$.

steps.slogan: Combine the graph description with the homomorphism laws for $f'$.
steps.detail: The image of $f$ is the graph of $f'$ by step 2, and $f'$ is a monoid homomorphism by steps 3 and 4. The graph of a monoid homomorphism is a [submonoid](c:submonoid) of $H \times I$, and it equals the image of $f$.

concepts.c:monoid-hom: The map $f$ and the function $f'$ are monoid homomorphisms, and $f$ gives $f(1) = (1, 1)$.
concepts.c:graph-of-a-function: The theorem says that the image of $f$ is the graph of $f'$.
concepts.c:submonoid: The image of a monoid homomorphism is a submonoid, here the graph of $f'$.

source.note: mathlib obtains $f'$ from exists_range_eq_graphOn_univ (a chosen preimage, well defined by the vertical line condition), then proves map_one and map_mul from membership in the image.

statement: Let $C$ be a [compact Riemann surface](c:compact-riemann-surface) of genus $g \ge 2$, and $k \ge 1$. The space of [conformal blocks](c:conformal-block) of the $SU(r)$ [WZW model](c:wess-zumino-witten-model) at level $k$ on $C$ is canonically isomorphic to $H^0(\mathcal{M}_C, \mathcal{L}^k)$, the level $k$ state space of 3d [Chern-Simons theory](c:d-3-chern-simons-theory). Here $\mathcal{M}_C$ is the moduli space of flat $SU(r)$-connections, with its complex structure from $C$.

hypotheses.text: $C$ is a [compact Riemann surface](c:compact-riemann-surface) of genus $g \ge 2$.
The gauge group is $SU(r)$ with $r \ge 2$, and its complexification is $SL_r(\mathbb{C})$.
The level $k$ is a positive integer.

conclusion: There is a canonical isomorphism from the space of [conformal blocks](c:conformal-block) of the level $k$ $SU(r)$ WZW model on $C$ onto $H^0(\mathcal{M}_C, \mathcal{L}^k)$, the Chern-Simons state space.

proofs.name: Conformal blocks as generalized theta functions
proofs.slogan: Uniformize the moduli stack by loop groups, so that sections of the determinant bundle become invariant forms on the basic representation, which are the conformal blocks.
proofs.scope: The correspondence between the two state spaces for $SU(r)$, as an outline resting on the cited work. Other members of the family (the full AdS$_3$/CFT$_2$ dictionary, partition functions, other groups $G$) are not covered.

roles.why: The surface $C$ and a point $p$ give the ring $A = \mathcal{O}(C \setminus p)$ and the uniformization of bundles.
The group $SL_r$ has the loop group, the affine Lie algebra and the basic representation that the steps use.
The level $k$ fixes the power $\mathcal{L}^k$ of the determinant bundle and the level of the vacuum representation.

steps.slogan: Describe the moduli stack of bundles as a double quotient of loop groups.
steps.detail: Fix a point $p \in C$ and put $A = \mathcal{O}(C \setminus p)$, $K = \mathbb{C}((z))$, $O = \mathbb{C}[[z]]$. Beauville and Laszlo glue bundles from trivializations and show that the stack of $SL_r$-bundles on $C$ is $SL_r(A) \backslash SL_r(K)/SL_r(O)$, the quotient of the [affine Grassmannian](c:affine-grassmannian) by $SL_r(A)$.

steps.slogan: Identify sections of the determinant bundle on the affine Grassmannian with a representation.
steps.detail: On the [affine Grassmannian](c:affine-grassmannian) $Q$, the space $H^0(Q, \mathcal{L}^k)$ is the dual $\mathcal{H}_k^*$ of the level $k$ vacuum representation of the [affine Lie algebra](c:affine-lie-algebra) $\widehat{\mathfrak{sl}}_r$ (Kumar, Mathieu).

steps.slogan: Take $SL_r(A)$-invariants to obtain the conformal blocks.
steps.detail: A section of $\mathcal{L}^k$ on the stack is an $SL_r(A)$-invariant section on $Q$, so an $\mathfrak{sl}_r(A)$-invariant linear form on $\mathcal{H}_k$. These forms are the dual of the coinvariants $\mathcal{H}_k/\mathfrak{sl}_r(A)\mathcal{H}_k$, that is, the space of [conformal blocks](c:conformal-block).

steps.slogan: Pass from the stack to the moduli space of semistable bundles.
steps.detail: The bundle $\mathcal{L}^k$ descends to the moduli space $SU_C(r)$ of semistable bundles, and sections on the stack equal sections on this space. So the invariants of step 3 are $H^0(SU_C(r), \mathcal{L}^k)$.

steps.slogan: Identify the moduli space with flat connections and read off the state space.
steps.detail: By the Narasimhan-Seshadri theorem, $SU_C(r)$ is the [moduli space of flat connections](c:moduli-space-of-flat-connections) of $SU(r)$ on the underlying surface, and $\mathcal{L}$ is the prequantum line bundle of its symplectic form. Kähler quantization at level $k$ gives $H^0(\mathcal{M}_C, \mathcal{L}^k)$, the state space of [Chern-Simons theory](c:d-3-chern-simons-theory).

concepts.c:compact-riemann-surface: The surface $C$ carries the complex structure that defines both state spaces.
concepts.c:conformal-block: Conformal blocks are the WZW side of the correspondence.
concepts.c:wess-zumino-witten-model: The WZW model on $C$ supplies the conformal blocks at level $k$.
concepts.c:d-3-chern-simons-theory: Its state space is the quantization of the moduli space of flat connections.
concepts.c:moduli-space-of-flat-connections: This space is the phase space that Chern-Simons theory quantizes.
concepts.c:affine-grassmannian: Bundles on $C$ are uniformized as the quotient of the affine Grassmannian.
concepts.c:affine-lie-algebra: Its vacuum representation of level $k$ carries the conformal blocks as invariant forms.

source.ref: A. Beauville and Y. Laszlo, Conformal blocks and generalized theta functions, Communications in Mathematical Physics 164 (1994), 385-419
source.note: Outline for SL_r. Kumar-Narasimhan-Ramanathan and Faltings (1994) extend the isomorphism to other groups; the Chern-Simons side uses Narasimhan-Seshadri and Kähler quantization.

statement: Let a consumer have smooth, strictly monotone, strictly convex and homothetic [preferences](c:preference-relation) over a high grade $H$ and a low grade $L$ of one good, at prices $p_H > p_L > 0$. Add the same amount $t > 0$ to both prices. If the optimal bundles are interior, the ratio $x_H / x_L$ of the optimal quantities rises, because the [relative price](c:relative-price-of-a-good) of the high grade falls.

hypotheses.text: The [preferences](c:preference-relation) are smooth, strictly monotone, strictly convex and homothetic.
The prices satisfy $p_H > p_L > 0$, and the same amount $t > 0$ is added to both.
Income is positive, and the optimal bundles before and after have $x_H > 0$ and $x_L > 0$.

conclusion: The optimal ratio $x_H/x_L$ at prices $(p_H + t, p_L + t)$ is strictly larger than at prices $(p_H, p_L)$.

proofs.name: Relative price and marginal rate
proofs.slogan: A fixed charge lowers the relative price of the high grade, and the optimal ratio of high to low grade rises as that price falls.
proofs.scope: The ordinary demand ratio under homothetic preferences, which have no income effect on the ratio. Without homotheticity the same steps along one indifference curve give the substitution effect only.

roles.why: Smoothness and strict convexity give the tangency condition, and homotheticity makes the marginal rate depend on the ratio only.
The inequality $p_L < p_H$ and $t > 0$ make the relative price fall.
An interior optimum satisfies the first-order condition of equal marginal rate and price ratio.

steps.slogan: Show that adding $t$ lowers the [relative price](c:relative-price-of-a-good) $p_H/p_L$.
steps.detail: Because $p_L < p_H$ and $t > 0$, we have $(p_H + t)\,p_L < p_H\,(p_L + t)$. Dividing by $p_L (p_L + t)$ gives $(p_H + t)/(p_L + t) < p_H/p_L$. The relative price of the high grade falls, although both prices rise.

steps.slogan: Write each interior optimum as a tangency of the budget line and an indifference curve.
steps.detail: At an interior optimum the marginal rate of substitution $m = u_H/u_L$ equals the price ratio $p_H/p_L$. For smooth, strictly monotone, strictly convex [preferences](c:preference-relation) this condition also characterizes the optimum.

steps.slogan: Use homotheticity to make the marginal rate a function of the ratio $r = x_H/x_L$.
steps.detail: Homothetic preferences have indifference curves that are scaled copies of one curve, so $m(\lambda x_H, \lambda x_L) = m(x_H, x_L)$. Hence $m = m(r)$ depends only on $r$. The optimum satisfies $m(r) = p_H/p_L$, so $r$ depends on the relative price and not on income.

steps.slogan: Show that the marginal rate $m(r)$ is a [strictly decreasing](c:monotone-function) function of $r$.
steps.detail: Write the indifference curve through $(1, 1)$ as $x_L = \varphi(x_H)$, with $\varphi' < 0$ and $\varphi'$ strictly increasing by strict monotonicity and strict convexity. Along it $m = -\varphi'(x_H)$ strictly decreases in $x_H$, while $r = x_H/\varphi(x_H)$ strictly increases. So $m$ is a strictly decreasing function of $r$.

steps.slogan: Compare the optimal ratios at the two relative prices.
steps.detail: Let $r_0$ and $r_1$ be the optimal ratios before and after. Then $m(r_0) = p_H/p_L$ and $m(r_1) = (p_H + t)/(p_L + t)$, and step 1 gives $m(r_1) < m(r_0)$. Since $m$ is strictly decreasing, $r_1 > r_0$.

concepts.c:preference-relation: The consumer's preferences give the marginal rate and the optimal bundle.
concepts.c:relative-price-of-a-good: The effect works through the fall of the relative price of the high grade.
concepts.c:monotone-function: The strictly decreasing marginal rate turns a lower price ratio into a higher quantity ratio.

source.note: A calculus form of the argument of Alchian and Allen, University Economics (1964): a fixed per-unit charge lowers the relative price of the better grade.

new_concepts.name: relative price of a good
new_concepts.reminder: The relative price of a good is its price divided by the price of another good.
new_concepts.definition: For goods $H$ and $L$ with prices $p_H$ and $p_L > 0$, the relative price of $H$ is $p_H/p_L$, the number of units of $L$ given up to buy one unit of $H$. A consumer with fixed income who has convex preferences chooses the bundle whose marginal rate of substitution equals this number.

statement: Let $E \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be bounded. Then $E$ lies in a [rectifiable curve](c:rectifiable-curve) iff $\sum_Q \beta_E(3Q)^2\,\ell(Q) < \infty$, over dyadic squares $Q$ of side $\ell(Q)$. Here $\beta_E(Q) = \inf_L \sup_{x \in E \cap Q} \mathrm{dist}(x, L)/\ell(Q)$ over lines $L$. The least length of such a curve is comparable to $\mathrm{diam}\,E + \sum_Q \beta_E(3Q)^2\,\ell(Q)$.

hypotheses.text: The set $E \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ is bounded.

conclusion: $E$ lies in a curve of finite length iff the beta sum is finite, and then the least length is comparable to $\mathrm{diam}\,E$ plus the sum, with absolute constants.

proofs.name: Jones's beta-number proof
proofs.slogan: Pythagoras bounds the beta sum by the length of any curve through $E$, and a scale-by-scale construction builds a curve whose length is bounded by the sum.
proofs.scope: The planar case (Jones, 1990), as an outline that rests on the cited paper. The versions for $\mathbb{R}^n$ (Okikiolu) and for Hilbert space (Schul) are not proved here.

roles.why: A bounded set has finite diameter, finite nets at each scale, and Hausdorff-limit compactness for the construction.

steps.slogan: Show that a curve through a square with beta number $\beta$ is long.
steps.detail: Let $\Gamma$ be a connected set containing $E$. Suppose $\Gamma$ joins two points $a, b \in 3Q$ that are at least $c\,\ell(Q)$ apart, and passes through a point of $E$ at distance $\ge \beta\,\ell(Q)$ from the line $ab$. By the Pythagorean theorem, the length of $\Gamma \cap 3Q$ exceeds $|a - b|$ by at least $c'\beta^2 \ell(Q)$.

steps.slogan: Add the excess lengths over all scales to bound the sum by the length.
steps.detail: Approximate $\Gamma$ by polygons $P_n$ through points of $E$ at scale $2^{-n}$. From $P_n$ to $P_{n+1}$ the length grows by at least $c\sum_{Q \in \mathcal{D}_n} \beta_E(3Q)^2 \ell(Q)$, and the enlarged squares overlap boundedly. Summing over $n$ gives $\sum_Q \beta_E(3Q)^2 \ell(Q) \le C\,\mathrm{length}(\Gamma)$.

steps.slogan: Build a connected polygonal set at each scale through a net of $E$.
steps.detail: For each $n$ take a maximal $2^{-n}$-separated net $E_n \subset E$. Build connected polygonal sets $\Gamma_n \supset E_n$ so that $\Gamma_{n+1}$ comes from $\Gamma_n$ by adding detours and short connecting segments near the squares of scale $2^{-n}$.

steps.slogan: Bound the length added at each scale by the beta numbers.
steps.detail: Near a square $Q$ with small $\beta_E(3Q)$, the net points lie close to a line, so by Pythagoras the detours cost at most $C\beta_E(3Q)^2 \ell(Q)$, up to terms controlled by the same sum. Hence $\mathrm{length}(\Gamma_n) \le C\,(\mathrm{diam}\,E + \sum_Q \beta_E(3Q)^2 \ell(Q))$ for every $n$.

steps.slogan: Take a limit of the polygonal sets to get a curve that contains $E$.
steps.detail: By the Blaschke selection theorem, a subsequence of $\Gamma_n$ converges in the Hausdorff metric to a compact connected set $\Gamma$. It contains $E$, because the nets $E_n$ become dense in $E$. By Gołąb's theorem, the [Hausdorff measure](c:hausdorff-measure) $\mathcal{H}^1(\Gamma)$ is at most $\liminf \mathrm{length}(\Gamma_n)$, so $\Gamma$ lies on a curve of finite length.

steps.slogan: Combine both directions into the characterization of subsets of curves.
steps.detail: If $E$ lies in a curve $\Gamma$ of finite length, step 2 gives a finite beta sum. If the sum is finite, step 5 gives a curve of finite length that contains $E$. Both steps carry explicit constants, so the least length is comparable to $\mathrm{diam}\,E$ plus the sum.

concepts.c:rectifiable-curve: The theorem says which sets lie on a curve of finite length.
concepts.c:hausdorff-measure: Length of the limit set is its one-dimensional Hausdorff measure.

source.ref: P. W. Jones, Rectifiable sets and the traveling salesman problem, Inventiones Mathematicae 102 (1990), 1-15
source.note: Outline of Jones's proof in the plane; the constants and the treatment of isolated points and spurs are in the paper.

statement: Let $V$ be a [Stein manifold](c:stein-manifold) of complex dimension $n$. Then $V$ is [homotopy equivalent](c:homotopy-equivalence) to a [CW complex](c:cw-complex) of real dimension at most $n$. In particular this holds for a smooth affine variety of dimension $n$ over $\mathbb{C}$.

hypotheses.text: $V$ is a [Stein manifold](c:stein-manifold).
The complex dimension of $V$ is $n$.

conclusion: $V$ has the homotopy type of a CW complex whose cells have dimension at most $n$.

proofs.name: Morse index bound
proofs.slogan: A strictly plurisubharmonic Morse function has critical points of index at most $n$, so Morse theory builds $V$ from cells of dimension at most $n$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, including $n = 0$, where $V$ is a discrete set of points. The case of a smooth affine variety follows because it is Stein.

roles.why: A Stein manifold carries a proper strictly plurisubharmonic function, which is the Morse function of the proof.
The real dimension $2n$ bounds the sum of the dimensions of a negative subspace $N$ and its image $JN$.

steps.slogan: Choose a smooth strictly plurisubharmonic proper function on $V$.
steps.detail: A [Stein manifold](c:stein-manifold) carries a smooth proper function $\rho\colon V \to [0, \infty)$ whose Levi form is positive definite at every point (strict plurisubharmonicity). For a closed complex submanifold of $\mathbb{C}^r$ one may take $\rho(z) = |z - p|^2$.

steps.slogan: Perturb the function into a [Morse function](c:morse-function) that keeps both properties.
steps.detail: Morse functions are dense in the $C^2$ fine topology, by Sard's theorem. Properness and positivity of the Levi form are open conditions in that topology. So we may assume that $\rho$ is Morse, proper, bounded below and strictly plurisubharmonic.

steps.slogan: Bound the index of every [critical point](c:critical-point) of $\rho$ by $n$.
steps.detail: At a critical point, the real [Hessian](c:hessian) $h$ satisfies $h(v) + h(Jv) > 0$ for $v \ne 0$, since this sum is a positive multiple of the Levi form. If $h < 0$ on a subspace $N$, then $N \cap JN = 0$: a vector $v = Jw$ with $v, w \in N$ would give $h(v) + h(Jv) = h(v) + h(-w) < 0$. So $2\dim N \le 2n$ and the index is at most $n$.

steps.slogan: Attach one cell for each critical point, with dimension equal to its index.
steps.detail: Because $\rho$ is proper and bounded below, every sublevel set $\{\rho \le a\}$ is compact. Morse theory then gives that $V$ is homotopy equivalent to a [CW complex](c:cw-complex) with one cell of dimension $\lambda$ for each critical point of index $\lambda$ (Milnor, Theorem 3.5, via the Morse lemma). By step 3, every $\lambda \le n$.

concepts.c:stein-manifold: Steinness provides the proper strictly plurisubharmonic function used throughout.
concepts.c:homotopy-equivalence: The conclusion identifies the homotopy type of $V$, not its homeomorphism type.
concepts.c:cw-complex: Morse theory builds the CW complex with one cell for each critical point.
concepts.c:morse-function: A Morse function has nondegenerate critical points, each giving one cell.
concepts.c:critical-point: Critical points carry the indices that fix the cell dimensions.
concepts.c:hessian: The Hessian at a critical point defines the index and relates to the Levi form.

source.note: The argument of Andreotti and Frankel (1959), as in Milnor, Morse Theory, section 7 and Theorem 3.5, with a strictly plurisubharmonic exhaustion of a Stein manifold.

statement: The quotient of the [complex projective plane](c:complex-projective-plane) $\mathbb{CP}^2$ by the involution $\tau[z] = [\bar z]$ is [homeomorphic](c:homeomorphism) to the 4-[sphere](c:sphere) $S^4$.

hypotheses.text: The involution $\tau$ of $\mathbb{CP}^2$ is [complex conjugation](c:complex-conjugation) of homogeneous coordinates: $[z_0{:}z_1{:}z_2] \mapsto [\bar z_0{:}\bar z_1{:}\bar z_2]$.

proofs.name: Real part of the projector
proofs.slogan: Send $[z]$ to the real part of the rank-one projector $zz^*$, which identifies $\mathbb{CP}^2/\tau$ with the boundary of a five-dimensional convex body.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The fixed points of $\tau$, the real projective plane, correspond to the rank-one matrices.

roles.why: Conjugation changes $y$ to $-y$ in $z = x + iy$, which leaves $xx^T + yy^T$ unchanged, and it accounts for the reflections in step 3.

steps.slogan: Send a unit vector $z = x + iy$ to the real symmetric matrix $xx^T + yy^T$.
steps.detail: For $|z| = 1$ put $\Phi(z) = \mathrm{Re}(zz^*) = xx^T + yy^T$. This is a real [symmetric matrix](c:symmetric-matrix), [positive semidefinite](c:positive-semidefinite-matrix), with trace $1$ and rank at most $2$. It is unchanged by a phase factor and by conjugation, so it gives a continuous map $\bar\Phi\colon \mathbb{CP}^2/\tau \to K$, where $K$ is the set of such matrices.

steps.slogan: Show that every matrix in $K$ is a value of the map.
steps.detail: Let $A \in K$. The spectral theorem gives $A = \lambda_1 u_1 u_1^T + \lambda_2 u_2 u_2^T$ with orthonormal $u_1, u_2$, $\lambda_k \ge 0$ and $\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 = 1$. Then $z = \sqrt{\lambda_1}\,u_1 + i\sqrt{\lambda_2}\,u_2$ is a unit vector with $\Phi(z) = A$.

steps.slogan: Show that equal values force the same point up to conjugation.
steps.detail: Let $\Phi(z) = \Phi(w) = A$. If $A$ has rank $2$, write $A = MM^T = M'M'^T$ with $M = [x\ y]$, $M' = [x'\ y']$ of rank $2$. Then $M' = MQ$ with $Q \in O(2)$, and $Q(1, i)^T$ is a phase times $(1, i)^T$ for a rotation, and a phase times $(1, -i)^T$ for a reflection. So $w = e^{i\theta}z$ or $w = e^{i\theta}\bar z$. If $A$ has rank $1$, both points are the real point $[u]$ with $A = uu^T$.

steps.slogan: Identify $K$ with the boundary of a [convex body](c:convex-body).
steps.detail: The set $P$ of positive semidefinite real symmetric matrices of trace $1$ is a compact [convex body](c:convex-body) in a $5$-dimensional affine space. Its interior is the set of positive definite matrices, so its boundary is $K$, the singular ones. Radial projection from $I/3$ is a homeomorphism from $K$ onto $S^4$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the induced bijection is a homeomorphism onto the sphere.
steps.detail: By steps 1 to 3, $\bar\Phi$ is a continuous bijection from $\mathbb{CP}^2/\tau$ onto $K$. The quotient is compact because $\mathbb{CP}^2$ is, and $K$ is [Hausdorff](c:hausdorff-space), so $\bar\Phi$ is a homeomorphism. Composing with step 4 gives $\mathbb{CP}^2/\tau \cong S^4$.

concepts.c:complex-projective-plane: The plane $\mathbb{CP}^2$ is the space whose quotient is identified.
concepts.c:homeomorphism: The theorem asserts a homeomorphism between the quotient and the sphere.
concepts.c:sphere: The target $S^4$ is the boundary sphere of a convex body.
concepts.c:complex-conjugation: Conjugation is the involution that the quotient divides out.
concepts.c:quotient-space: The quotient by $\tau$ is a compact space that the map $\bar\Phi$ describes.
concepts.c:symmetric-matrix: The real part of the projector is a real symmetric matrix.
concepts.c:positive-semidefinite-matrix: Positive semidefiniteness with trace one defines the convex body and the set $K$.
concepts.c:convex-body: A compact convex body with interior has a boundary homeomorphic to a sphere.
concepts.c:hausdorff-space: A continuous bijection from a compact space onto a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism.

source.note: The theorem is due to Arnold, Kuiper and Massey (1970s); this is an elementary proof by the map $z \mapsto \mathrm{Re}(zz^*)$.

statement: Let $u$ be $C^2$ with $u' > 0$ near the wealth $w$, and let $Y$ be a bounded [random variable](c:random-variable) with [expected value](c:expected-value) $\mu$. Let $N$ identical individuals with wealth $w$ each receive the share $Y/N$. The [risk premium](c:risk-premium-of-a-gamble) $\pi_N$ defined by $u(w + \mu/N - \pi_N) = \mathbb{E}\,u(w + Y/N)$ obeys $\pi_N = O(1/N^2)$, so the total cost of [risk](c:risk), $N\pi_N$, tends to $0$.

hypotheses.text: The utility $u$ is twice continuously differentiable with $u' > 0$ on an interval around the wealth $w$.
The net benefit $Y$ is a bounded [random variable](c:random-variable) with [expected value](c:expected-value) $\mu$.
The net benefit is shared equally among $N$ identical individuals with the same constant wealth $w$ and the same utility $u$.

conclusion: The [risk premium](c:risk-premium-of-a-gamble) of each share is $O(1/N^2)$, so the total [risk](c:risk) cost $N\pi_N$ tends to $0$ as $N \to \infty$.

proofs.name: Second-order expansion of the premium
proofs.slogan: Expand both the expected utility of a share and the utility of its certainty equivalent to second order, and compare them.
proofs.scope: Constant baseline wealth, a bounded benefit, and shares of size $Y/N$ (returns independent of the individuals' other income). If the returns correlate with income, the premium need not vanish.

roles.why: Smoothness gives the second-order expansions, and $u'(w) > 0$ lets us divide by $u'(w)$ and define the certainty equivalent.
Boundedness of $Y$ bounds the remainders by $\tfrac12 M B^2 s^2$ and keeps the certainty equivalent near $w$.
Equal shares of size $Y/N$ give the small scale $s = 1/N$, and the premium of the whole group is $N$ times that of one share.

steps.slogan: Define the certainty equivalent of one share and bound its distance from $w$.
steps.detail: Let $|Y| \le B$ and $s = 1/N$, small enough that $I = [w - Bs, w + Bs]$ lies where $u' > 0$. Then $u$ increases on $I$, so $\mathbb{E}\,u(w + sY) \in [u(w - Bs), u(w + Bs)]$, and some $c \in I$ has $u(c) = \mathbb{E}\,u(w + sY)$. The [risk premium](c:risk-premium-of-a-gamble) is $\pi_N = w + s\mu - c$, and $|c - w| \le Bs$.

steps.slogan: Expand the expected utility of the share to second order.
steps.detail: Let $M$ bound $|u''|$ on a fixed interval around $w$. Taylor's theorem gives $u(w + sY) = u(w) + s\,u'(w)\,Y + R$ with $|R| \le \tfrac12 M B^2 s^2$. Taking [expected values](c:expected-value), $\mathbb{E}\,u(w + sY) = u(w) + s\,u'(w)\,\mu + R_1$ with $|R_1| \le \tfrac12 M B^2 s^2$.

steps.slogan: Expand the utility of the certainty equivalent to second order.
steps.detail: Since $|c - w| \le Bs$, Taylor's theorem gives $u(c) = u(w) + u'(w)(c - w) + R_2$ with $|R_2| \le \tfrac12 M B^2 s^2$. Here $c - w = s\mu - \pi_N$.

steps.slogan: Equate the two expansions and solve for the risk premium.
steps.detail: From $u(c) = \mathbb{E}\,u(w + sY)$ we get $u'(w)(s\mu - \pi_N) + R_2 = s\,u'(w)\,\mu + R_1$. Hence $u'(w)\,\pi_N = R_2 - R_1$, and $|\pi_N| \le M B^2 s^2 / u'(w)$ because $u'(w) > 0$.

steps.slogan: Multiply the premium by $N$ to get the total cost of [risk](c:risk).
steps.detail: The $N$ individuals bear $N\pi_N$ in total, and $|N\pi_N| \le M B^2/(u'(w)\,N)$. This tends to $0$ as $N \to \infty$, so the project may be judged by its expected net benefit $\mu$ alone.

concepts.c:random-variable: The net benefit of the project is a bounded random variable.
concepts.c:expected-value: The mean $\mu$ of the benefit and the expected utility are the quantities compared.
concepts.c:risk: The cost of risk is what the theorem shows to vanish as the population grows.
concepts.c:risk-premium-of-a-gamble: The premium measures the cost of risk that one individual bears for a share.

source.note: The expansion argument behind Arrow and Lind, Uncertainty and the evaluation of public investment decisions, American Economic Review 60 (1970), in the Arrow-Pratt form with a Taylor remainder.

new_concepts.name: risk premium of a gamble
new_concepts.reminder: The risk premium of a gamble is the amount by which its expected value exceeds its certainty equivalent.
new_concepts.definition: For a utility $u$, wealth $w$ and gamble $G$, the certainty equivalent $c$ solves $u(c) = \mathbb{E}\,u(w + G)$, and the risk premium is $w + \mathbb{E}\,G - c$. It is nonnegative for every gamble if and only if $u$ is concave.

statement: Let $G$ be a [finite group](c:finite-group) whose [Sylow](c:sylow-subgroup) $2$-subgroup $S$ is [generalized quaternion](c:generalized-quaternion-group), and assume that $G$ has no nontrivial [normal subgroup](c:normal-subgroup) of odd order. Then the center $Z(G)$ has order $2$. In particular $G$ is not simple.

hypotheses.text: $G$ is a [finite group](c:finite-group).
A Sylow $2$-subgroup $S$ of $G$ is a [generalized quaternion group](c:generalized-quaternion-group).
$G$ has no nontrivial normal subgroup of odd order, that is, $O(G) = 1$.

conclusion: The center of $G$ has order $2$, so $G$ is not simple.

proofs.name: Principal 2-block argument
proofs.slogan: The involution of the Sylow subgroup acts as a scalar on the principal $2$-block, whose characters cut out $O(G)$, so it is central.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, as an outline: step 4 rests on the cited papers. The Z* theorem of Glauberman generalizes the result, but its proof uses the Brauer-Suzuki theorem, so it is not used here.

roles.why: Finiteness gives Sylow subgroups, characters and Brauer's blocks.
A generalized quaternion group has a unique involution $z$, which is central in $S$ and has no other conjugate in $S$.
The condition $O(G) = 1$ makes $Z(G)$ a $2$-group and makes the principal block faithful on $G$.

steps.slogan: Reduce the claim to showing that the involution of $S$ is central.
steps.detail: The odd part of $Z(G)$ is normal in $G$ and of odd order, so it is trivial, and $Z(G)$ is a $2$-group. By [Sylow's theorems](c:sylow-subgroup) it lies in $S$ and centralizes $S$, so $Z(G) \le Z(S) = \langle z \rangle$, where $z$ is the unique involution of $S$. Hence $|Z(G)| = 2$ exactly when $z \in Z(G)$.

steps.slogan: Note that $z$ has no other conjugate inside $S$.
steps.detail: A generalized quaternion group has exactly one involution $z$, and $Z(S) = \langle z \rangle$. Every $G$-conjugate of $z$ that lies in $S$ is an involution of $S$, so it equals $z$. Thus $z$ is the only element of $S$ in its $G$-class.

steps.slogan: Pass to the principal $2$-block, whose characters cut out $O(G)$.
steps.detail: In Brauer's [modular representation](c:modular-representation) theory, the principal $2$-block $B_0$ of $G$ has defect group $S$. The intersection of the kernels of the irreducible characters in $B_0$ is $O(G)$, which is trivial here. So these [characters](c:character-of-a-representation) together separate the elements of $G$.

steps.slogan: Show that $z$ acts as a scalar in every representation of the principal block.
steps.detail: Brauer and Suzuki study the characters of $B_0$ by Brauer's theory of blocks whose defect group is generalized quaternion, with $z$ the unique involution of the defect group. They show that $\chi(z) = \pm\chi(1)$ for every $\chi \in B_0$, so $z$ acts as the scalar $\pm 1$. The cited papers carry out this step.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $z$ is central, so $Z(G)$ has order $2$.
steps.detail: If $z$ acts as a scalar in the representation of $\chi \in B_0$, every commutator $[z, g]$ acts trivially and lies in $\ker\chi$. So $[z, g] \in O(G) = 1$ for all $g$, and $z \in Z(G)$. With step 1, $|Z(G)| = 2$. Since $|G| \ge |S| \ge 8 > 2$, the center is a proper nontrivial normal subgroup, so $G$ is not simple.

concepts.c:finite-group: Finiteness gives Sylow subgroups and the character theory used.
concepts.c:sylow-subgroup: The Sylow $2$-subgroup $S$ and its conjugates control the central involution.
concepts.c:generalized-quaternion-group: Its unique involution is central in $S$ and has no other conjugate there.
concepts.c:normal-subgroup: Normal subgroups of odd order are excluded, and the center is normal.
concepts.c:modular-representation: Brauer's blocks come from the modular representation theory of $G$.
concepts.c:character-of-a-representation: Characters of the principal block detect $z$ and cut out $O(G)$.

source.ref: R. Brauer and M. Suzuki, On finite groups of even order whose 2-Sylow group is a quaternion group, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 45 (1959), 1757-1759; R. Brauer, Some applications of the theory of blocks of characters of finite groups I, Journal of Algebra 1 (1964), 152-167
source.note: Outline of the block-theoretic proof; The theorem is credited to Brauer and Suzuki (1959), Suzuki (1962) and Brauer (1964). Step 4 is the content of the cited papers.

statement: The only solution of the [Diophantine equation](c:diophantine-equation) $x^a - y^b = 1$ in integers $x, y > 0$ and $a, b > 1$ is $x = 3$, $y = 2$, $a = 2$, $b = 3$. That is, $8$ and $9$ are the only consecutive perfect powers.

hypotheses.text: The integers $x$ and $y$ are positive.
The exponents $a$ and $b$ are integers greater than $1$.
The integers satisfy the [Diophantine equation](c:diophantine-equation) $x^a - y^b = 1$.

conclusion: The solution is $(x, y, a, b) = (3, 2, 2, 3)$, that is, $3^2 - 2^3 = 1$.

proofs.name: Mihăilescu's cyclotomic proof
proofs.slogan: Reduce to prime exponents, settle exponent $2$ classically, and exclude two odd primes by cyclotomic fields, the Stickelberger ideal and primary cyclotomic units.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, as an outline: steps 3 to 6 rest on the cited paper and on Bilu's account of it. The related conjectures of Pillai and Fermat-Catalan are not covered.

roles.why: Positive bases let the divisibility relations of Cassels and the factorization in the cyclotomic field apply.
Exponents above $1$ allow a reduction to prime exponents and rule out the trivial cases.
The equation gives the factorization $x^p - 1 = y^q$ that all later steps study.

steps.slogan: Reduce to prime exponents $p$ and $q$.
steps.detail: Choose [primes](c:prime-number) $p \mid a$ and $q \mid b$. Then $(x^{a/p})^p - (y^{b/q})^q = 1$ is a solution with prime exponents. So it suffices to find all solutions of $x^p - y^q = 1$ with $p, q$ prime, and then to recover $a$ and $b$.

steps.slogan: Settle the cases with an exponent equal to $2$ by classical arguments.
steps.detail: Lebesgue (1850) showed that $x^p = y^2 + 1$ has no solution with $y \ne 0$. For $x^2 = y^q + 1$, Euler and Ko Chao (1965) show that the only solution is $3^2 - 2^3 = 1$. This leaves $p$ and $q$ odd primes.

steps.slogan: Show that each exponent divides the base of the other power.
steps.detail: For odd primes $p, q$ and a solution of $x^p - y^q = 1$, Cassels (1960) proved that $q \mid x$ and $p \mid y$. All later steps use these divisibilities together with the factorization $x^p - 1 = y^q$.

steps.slogan: Derive the double Wieferich congruences for the pair $(p, q)$.
steps.detail: Mihăilescu proved that $p^{q-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{q^2}$ and $q^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p^2}$. His argument factors $y^q = \prod_j (x - \zeta^j)$ in the [cyclotomic field](c:cyclotomic-field) $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)$ and uses Cassels' divisibilities and cyclotomic units.

steps.slogan: Restrict the pair $(p, q)$ with the Stickelberger ideal and Thaine's theorem.
steps.detail: The Stickelberger ideal annihilates the class group of $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)$, and Thaine's theorem turns this into information on $p$-th powers of cyclotomic units. Mihăilescu uses it to show that $p \equiv 1 \pmod q$ or $q \equiv 1 \pmod p$.

steps.slogan: Rule out both congruences with the plus argument on primary cyclotomic units.
steps.detail: Mihăilescu studies the plus part of the group of cyclotomic units of $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)$ that are $q$-th powers. This plus argument shows that neither congruence of step 5 can hold, which contradicts step 5. So no solution has two odd prime exponents.

steps.slogan: Combine the exponent-$2$ case with the exclusion of two odd primes.
steps.detail: The exponent-$2$ cases leave only $3^2 - 2^3 = 1$, and no solution has two odd prime exponents. By step 1, any solution of the original equation gives such a solution with prime exponents. Since $3$ and $2$ are not perfect powers, $(x, y, a, b) = (3, 2, 2, 3)$.

concepts.c:diophantine-equation: The theorem solves this equation in perfect powers.
concepts.c:prime-number: The reduction passes to prime exponents, where Cassels' relations hold.
concepts.c:cyclotomic-field: The factorization of $x^p - 1$ in $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)$ drives the proof.

source.ref: P. Mihăilescu, Primary cyclotomic units and a proof of Catalan's conjecture, Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik 572 (2004), 167-195
source.note: Outline after Mihăilescu and Bilu, Catalan's conjecture (after Mihăilescu), Séminaire Bourbaki 909, Astérisque 294 (2004): Cassels relations, double Wieferich criterion, plus argument.

statement: Let $G$ be a smooth connected [algebraic group](c:algebraic-group) over a [perfect field](c:perfect-field) $k$. Then $G$ has a unique smooth connected affine [normal subgroup](c:normal-subgroup) $H$ such that $G/H$ is an [abelian variety](c:abelian-variety).

hypotheses.text: The field $k$ is [perfect](c:perfect-field).
$G$ is a smooth connected [algebraic group](c:algebraic-group) over $k$.

conclusion: There is exactly one smooth connected affine normal subgroup $H \le G$ for which $G/H$ is an [abelian variety](c:abelian-variety).

proofs.name: Largest affine normal subgroup
proofs.slogan: Take the largest affine normal subgroup, show that the quotient is proper hence abelian, then prove uniqueness and descend to $k$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, as an outline: step 3 rests on the cited work. The statement fails over imperfect fields, where the affine subgroup need not be smooth or defined over $k$.

roles.why: Perfectness makes $\bar k/k$ Galois, so the unique subgroup over $\bar k$ descends to $k$.
Smoothness and connectedness make the products of subgroups smooth and connected, and give the properness step.

steps.slogan: Find the largest smooth connected affine normal subgroup of $G_{\bar k}$.
steps.detail: Over $\bar k$, if $H_1$ and $H_2$ are smooth connected affine [normal subgroups](c:normal-subgroup), then $H_1 H_2$, the image of $H_1 \times H_2$, is another one. Take one of maximal dimension. It contains all the others, and we call it $H$.

steps.slogan: Divide by $H$ to get a group with no nontrivial such subgroup.
steps.detail: Let $N \le G/H$ be smooth, connected, affine and normal. Its preimage in $G$ is an extension of $N$ by $H$, so it is affine, smooth, connected and normal. By maximality it equals $H$, so $N = 1$.

steps.slogan: Show that a group without such a subgroup is proper.
steps.detail: This is the hard step. Chevalley's proof uses the map from the group to its Albanese variety. Rosenlicht and Conrad analyse the group directly, and Conrad uses a compactification of the group and descent theory. The result is that $G/H$ is proper.

steps.slogan: Identify the proper smooth connected group $G/H$ as an [abelian variety](c:abelian-variety).
steps.detail: A smooth connected proper group variety is commutative, by the rigidity lemma, and it is projective. So $G/H$ is an [abelian variety](c:abelian-variety).

steps.slogan: Prove uniqueness, using that an affine proper connected group is trivial.
steps.detail: Let $H'$ be another smooth connected affine normal subgroup with $G/H'$ an abelian variety. Then $H' \le H$ by maximality. The quotient $H/H'$ is a closed subgroup of $G/H'$, so it is proper, and it is affine as a quotient of $H$. An affine proper connected variety is a point, so $H = H'$.

steps.slogan: Descend from $\bar k$ to $k$ using that $k$ is perfect.
steps.detail: Since $k$ is [perfect](c:perfect-field), $\bar k/k$ is Galois. For $\sigma \in \mathrm{Gal}(\bar k/k)$ the subgroup $\sigma(H)$ has the same properties, so uniqueness gives $\sigma(H) = H$. Galois descent gives a smooth connected affine normal subgroup of $G$ over $k$ with abelian variety quotient, unique by step 5.

concepts.c:algebraic-group: The theorem describes the structure of such a group.
concepts.c:perfect-field: Perfectness makes the algebraic closure Galois, so descent works.
concepts.c:abelian-variety: The quotient by the affine subgroup is a proper commutative group variety.
concepts.c:normal-subgroup: Normality of the affine subgroup allows the quotient and the product of two subgroups.

source.ref: B. Conrad, A modern proof of Chevalley's theorem on algebraic groups, Journal of the Ramanujan Mathematical Society 17 (2002), 1-18
source.note: Outline of Rosenlicht's proof as presented by Conrad; Chevalley, Barsotti and Rosenlicht proved the theorem in the 1950s, and Milne's exposition (arXiv 1311.6060) follows Rosenlicht.

statement: Let $T$ be a [recursively enumerable](c:recursively-enumerable-set) set of sentences of a [first-order](c:first-order-logic) language with computable syntax. Then some primitive recursive set $T'$ of sentences has the same logical consequences as $T$. So $T$ has a decidable [axiomatization](c:axiomatization).

hypotheses.text: $T$ is a [recursively enumerable set](c:recursively-enumerable-set) of sentences.
The language is first-order, and its formulas are coded by natural numbers through a computable [Gödel numbering](c:godel-numbering).

conclusion: There is a primitive recursive set $T'$ of sentences with the same logical consequences as $T$.

proofs.name: Craig's padding trick
proofs.slogan: Enumerate the theory by a primitive recursive function, and replace its $m$-th value by a conjunction of $m$ copies, so that membership is decidable by a bounded search.
proofs.scope: All nonempty $T$; for $T = \emptyset$ take $T' = \emptyset$. The polynomial-time version needs a longer padding and is not proved here.

roles.why: Enumerability gives a primitive recursive function whose range is $T$, by the Kleene normal form.
Computable coding lets us build the padded sentences and compare them with a given sentence by a primitive recursive search.

steps.slogan: Write the set $T$ as the range of a primitive recursive function.
steps.detail: By the Kleene normal form, $\varphi \in T$ iff $R(\varphi, n)$ holds for some $n$, with $R$ primitive recursive. Fix $\varphi_0 \in T$, and define $g(\langle\varphi, n\rangle) = \varphi$ if $R(\varphi, n)$, and $g(\langle\varphi, n\rangle) = \varphi_0$ otherwise. Then $g$ is primitive recursive and has range $T$.

steps.slogan: Replace each value $g(m)$ by a conjunction of $m$ copies of it.
steps.detail: For $m \ge 1$ let $\theta_m = \varphi \wedge (\varphi \wedge (\dots \wedge \varphi))$ with $m$ copies of $\varphi = g(m)$. Put $T' = \{\theta_m : m \ge 1\}$. The sentence $\theta_m$ has length at least $m$.

steps.slogan: Decide membership in $T'$ by a bounded search.
steps.detail: Given a sentence $\psi$ of length $\ell$, test each $m \le \ell$: compute $g(m)$, build $\theta_m$ and compare it with $\psi$. Then $\psi \in T'$ iff some test succeeds, because $\theta_m$ has length at least $m$. Every operation is primitive recursive, so $T'$ is a primitive recursive set.

steps.slogan: Show that $T'$ and $T$ have the same consequences.
steps.detail: Each $\theta_m$ is logically equivalent to $g(m) \in T$, so every element of $T'$ follows from $T$. Every $\varphi \in T$ equals $g(m)$ for some $m$, so $\theta_m \in T'$ implies $\varphi$. Hence the two sets have the same consequences.

steps.slogan: Combine decidability and equivalence into one [axiomatization](c:axiomatization).
steps.detail: By steps 3 and 4, $T'$ is a primitive recursive set that axiomatizes the theory generated by $T$. So the theory has a decidable axiomatization, even though $T$ itself may be undecidable.

concepts.c:recursively-enumerable-set: Enumerability of $T$ is the hypothesis that the padding trick turns into decidability.
concepts.c:first-order-logic: In first-order logic a conjunction of copies of a sentence is equivalent to the sentence.
concepts.c:axiomatization: The set $T'$ is a simpler axiomatization of the theory of $T$.
concepts.c:godel-numbering: Coding makes sentence length, padding and comparison primitive recursive operations.

source.note: Craig's trick, from W. Craig, On axiomatizability within a system, Journal of Symbolic Logic 18 (1953), 30-32.
